newsitem.title: UK: Eurotunnel still faces challenge after debt deal.
newsitem.headline: Eurotunnel still faces challenge after debt deal.

text.p: Eurotunnel's huge debt accord will give the Channel Tunnel operator an opportunity over the next few years to get itself into financial shape and thrive in the competitive cross-Channel market, analysts said on Monday.
But experts said it was premature to predict the Anglo-French company's long-term survival, owing to the uncertainties of the transport market and the heavy debt burden Eurotunnel still carries.

"They are sustainable now, they can keep the tunnel running, but the long wait before they start facing up to their debts makes it very, very difficult to value the company," said one transport analyst at a large investment bank in London.
"Unless you really believe Eurotunnel is going to grow massively over the next few years it is hard to see the long-term valuations stacking up," added the analyst, who asked not to be named.

The key feature of the deal that Eurotunnel has struck with the leaders of its banking syndicate is that it allows the company to trim its annual interest bill and even postpone payment of some of this interest during the next few years, at no additional cost.
The principal on its junior debt, which has been more than halved to 4.0 billion pounds ($6.26 billion), will not be addressed until 2004.
Therefore, analysts said, the deal meant Eurotunnel's financial future would become sustainable for a time but it brought with it new risks linked to its future ability to pay.

The company estimated on Monday that its initial annual interest bill ould be about 400 million pounds. It has a war chest of up to 1.85 billion pounds of so-called stabilisation notes that it can use to settle any interest it cannot afford.
These notes are interest free until 2006.

"If you look at the current cash flow of between 150 and 200 million pounds a year, what they can't find (to meet the 400 million interest bill) they will roll forward into the stabilisation notes, and they can keep that going for seven, eight or nine years," another analyst said.
The key question is how the business develops during the restructuring period up to 2003, analysts said.
Mary-Ellen Collins of BDS Securities, said the debt plan appeared to be structured in anticipation of some kind of boom in revenue although she could not see the fundamentals justifying this.
"By all accounts it is unlikely that there will be a huge spurt of growth immediately," she told Reuters.

Her projections of Eurotunnel's earnings before interest, tax, depreciation and amortisation show it needing to call on several hundred million of its stabilisation notes in 1997, 1998 and even in 1999 to meet interest and senior debt commitments.
The calculations were based on modest growth forecasts, she added, but they suggested that over several years the company could use up to 1.5 billion pounds of what are effectively IOUs.
"They can't turn the operation around that quickly, so you could have banks sitting with a lot of stabilisation notes and a lot of debt not paying any interest," she added.

Eurotunnel's outgoing British chairman, Sir Alastair Morton, said he saw some hope for a boost to operating profits if, as he expected, the current phase of deep fare discounting by both the tunnel and its rival ferry companies ended soon.

He told reporters he hoped a planned joint venture between ferry operators P&O of Britain and Sweden's Stena Line would go ahead and bring with it rationalisation of ship capacity on the all-important Dover-Calais route.
Yet, although he said Eurotunnel could take a number of measures to increase its own capacity and rate of throughput in the coming years, he held back from forecasting strong growth. ($1=.6393 Pound)
